newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. hails UN refugee body reforms, gives cash.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hails UN refugee body reforms, gives cash.

text.p: The United States, a fierce critic of alleged United Nations bureaucracy, on Monday hailed reforms under way at the UNHCR refugee agency and reported it had raised its contributions to the body during 1996.

Assistant Secretary of State Phyllis Oakley told the UNHCR Executive Committee that Washington also hailed efforts by High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata, who heads the agency, to bring more women into the organisation.
"My government is tremendously impressed with UNHCR's pro-active efforts to "change management' and reform the organisation to respond more efficiently and effectively," Oakley said.
An action plan launched by Ogata "is now resulting in concrete changes in the way that UNHCR does its business," Oakley added.

She said she also wanted to pay tribute to Ogata and "to the work of thousands of UNHCR staff members who work every day to find solutions for the plight of the world's refugees," according to a text issued by the U.S. mission in Geneva.

The tone of her remarks contrasted sharply with official U.S. comment on the overall management of the U.N., whose Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali Washington has vowed to see stand down at the end of the year.

U.S. representatives argue reforms of the organisation launched by the former Egyptian deputy foreign minister since he took office in 1992 are not radical enough. He has said he will fight to stay on.

The United States has often been complimentary about the Geneva-based UNHCR, which currently has some 26 million refugees and displaced people around the world under its wing, according to figures Ogata gave to the Executive Committee on Monday.

The 69-year-old former Japanese academic, who has headed the agency through major humanitarian crises for nearly six years, has often been cited as a possible successor to Boutros-Ghali, but she has made clear she does not want the job.

Oakley told the UNHCR's 51-member Executive Committee she was happy to report that U.S. contributions to the agency in 1996 had surpassed those of 1995 by nearly $30 million, for a total of $254 million.
The United States is in debt to the tune of $1.65 billion dollars to the U.N. itself.
